meta.title: Who really said "Bubble bubble, toil and trouble"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shakespeare's witches say "Double, double toil and trouble; Fire burn and cauldron bubble" in Macbeth. "Bubble bubble" is a popular misquote found nowhere in the play.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Bubble bubble, toil and trouble'?
meta.ogDescription: It's a misquote of Macbeth. Shakespeare's witches chant "Double, double toil and trouble" — not "Bubble bubble." Here's the real line.

answer.label: Not quite Shakespeare — a misquote of Macbeth
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Shakespeare’s, but the wording is wrong. In ‘Macbeth’ (Act 4, Scene 1) the three witches chant “Double, double toil and trouble; Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.” “Bubble bubble” appears nowhere in the play — it is a popular misremembering that folds the closing word “bubble” back into the opening “double, double.”

trail: Shakespeare’s genuine refrain, “Double, double toil and trouble; Fire burn, and cauldron bubble,” appears in the MIT online Macbeth (4.1) and the Folger edition.
The “Bubble, bubble” form is a recognised error: one writer catalogues it as a misquote people routinely get wrong.
It also lands on lists of the most misremembered quotes from Macbeth.
source.excerptNote: The refrain recurs three times as the witches feed the cauldron. The familiar “Bubble bubble” version simply is not in the text.

author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright, poet and actor, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. His tragedy Macbeth, written around 1606, opens with three witches whose cauldron chant — “Double, double toil and trouble” — is among the most quoted (and misquoted) passages in all of English drama.

misattribution.heading: How “Double” became “Bubble”
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong author — the line really is Shakespeare’s. It is the wording that has drifted. The genuine refrain is “Double, double toil and trouble; Fire burn, and cauldron bubble,” and the popular “Bubble bubble, toil and trouble” collapses those two lines into one.

items.why: Ear and image conspire: the witches are literally bent over a bubbling cauldron, so “bubble” feels right — and it echoes the real closing word. But Shakespeare wrote “Double, double,” a deliberate doubling that mirrors the play’s theme of redoubling evil, per the MIT text of 4.1.
The refrain belongs to the three witches in Act 4, Scene 1 — so the attribution to Shakespeare is right even when the quotation is not.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare’s witches chant “Double, double toil and trouble; Fire burn, and cauldron bubble” — there is no “Bubble bubble” in the play.

context.heading: Why the line sticks
lead: The witches’ incantation is one of Shakespeare’s most incantatory passages — short, trochaic, and chanted in unison over a boiling cauldron. Its very catchiness is what makes it so easy to garble: the rhythm survives even when the words slip.

“Double, double” is doing real work. The repetition foreshadows the doubling of Macbeth’s crimes and the witches’ equivocation — their habit of saying things that mean two things at once. Flatten it to “Bubble bubble” and you keep the spooky music but lose the meaning.
context.pull: There is no “Bubble bubble” — only “Double, double.”
